title: Cauchy theorem and simply connected domains
section: Complex Variables ▷ Theorems Concerning Analytic Functions
terms: Cauchy theorem; simply connected domain; closed contour; primitive existence; contour deformation.

exposition.text:
A domain is a connected open subset of C. It is simply connected if every closed loop can be
continuously contracted to a point inside the domain. If f is holomorphic on a simply con-
nected domain, its integral around every piecewise smooth closed path is zero, and it has a
primitive.
The absence of singularities on the contour alone is insufficient: what lies inside, or the topol-
ogy of the domain, matters. The function 1/z is holomorphic on the punctured plane but inte-
grates to 2πi around a counterclockwise circle enclosing the origin. Contours can be deformed
through regions of holomorphy without changing the integral.

question.text:
Let f be holomorphic on 1 < |z| < 4. If its counterclockwise integral over |z| = 2 is 6πi, what is
its clockwise integral over |z| = 3?
(A) 0 (B) 3πi (C) 6πi (D) −6πi (E) 9πi

solution.text:
Cauchy’s theorem applied to the region between the circles makes the two counterclockwise
integrals equal. Reversing the outer orientation changes its sign, giving −6πi.

question.text:

Let D = C \ {−it : t ≥ 0}. For any piecewise smooth path C in D from −1 to 1, what is dz/z?
C
(A) 0
(B) πi
(C) −πi
(D) 2πi
(E) It can have different values for different paths in D.

solution.text:
On this slit plane choose the continuous argument in (−π/2, 3π/2). The logarithm
log |z| + i arg z is a primitive of 1/z. Its values at −1 and 1 are πi and zero, so the in-
tegral is −πi. The specified domain prevents paths from differing by a full turn around the
origin.

question.text:
On D = C \ {−1, 1} let f(z) = 1/(z − 1) − 1/(z + 1). Its integral around |z| = 2 is zero. Does it
have a single-valued primitive on D?
(A) Yes, because one closed contour integral vanishes.
(B) Yes, because both poles lie inside the same circle.
2
(C) Yes, with primitive log |z − 1|.
(D) No, because a small counterclockwise circle about 1 has integral 2πi.
(E) No, because f is not holomorphic on D.

solution.text:
The two contributions cancel on the large circle, but a sufficiently small circle centered
at one encloses only that pole and has integral 2πi. A global primitive would make every
closed-contour integral zero. The function is holomorphic on D; the obstruction comes from
the separate holes and their nonzero periods.

question.text:
Which assertion holds for every analytic function f on a simply connected open subset D of C?
(A) The function f is a polynomial.
(B) The integral of f is zero around every closed piecewise smooth curve in D.
(C) The function 1/f is analytic on D.
(D) The function f has no zeros.
(E) The function f is bounded.

solution.text:
Cauchy’s theorem on a simply connected domain makes every such closed-curve integral
zero, equivalently giving an analytic primitive. Boundedness, polynomial form, and absence
of zeros do not follow from analyticity on an arbitrary domain.
